Gamal Abdel Nasser. Egypt's second president from 1954 to 1970, and the architect of Arab nationalism and non-alignment in the Cold War. A military officer who led the 1952 revolution toppling the monarchy, he became the Arab world's most influential leader through anti-imperialism, socialist modernization, and the defiant Suez Crisis.

He led the Free Officers Movement that overthrew King Farouk in 1952, emerging as Egypt's strongman by 1954 and reshaping the nation as an Arab socialist state. In 1956, he nationalized the Suez Canal, triggering the Suez Crisis when Britain, France, and Israel invaded. He survived the attack and emerged a continental hero, cementing his pan-Arab leadership. He promoted Arab nationalism and unity, including the short-lived union with Syria called the United Arab Republic from 1958 to 1961, positioning Egypt as the leader of the Arab world against Israel and Western imperialism.

He expanded Egypt's military, built the Aswan High Dam to harness the Nile, and pursued rapid industrialization and land reform to modernize the nation. He aligned with the Soviet Union for military and economic support, becoming a key figure in non-aligned politics during the Cold War. He died in office in 1970, widely mourned across the Arab world as a symbol of dignity, resistance, and Arab power. Like Kwame Nkrumah and Haile Selassie, he was a contemporary African and Arab leader competing for continental influence and championing decolonization and anti-imperialism.
